where: Section 3, the Euclidean distance formula note
problem: The note says d 'is a distance in the same units as the features, here rupees'. That holds only when all D features share one unit. With mixed columns (spend in rupees, age in years, visits per month) the squares add quantities of different units and the distance has no single unit, so the note is misleading as a general definition.
fix: Add one sentence: when features carry different units, standardise each column first (subtract its mean, divide by its standard deviation) so the distance is meaningful; in the one-feature example here the unit is rupees.

problem: 'There is no y to compare against, so no error can be computed directly' clashes with Section 3, where k-means does minimise an objective (total squared distance to centres). A careful student will notice the contradiction.
fix: Say 'no error against a true answer can be computed', then note that we can still write our own objective, such as the total squared distance of points to their centres, and minimise that.

problem: 'The search for the minimum is backpropagation plus an optimiser' gives backprop the wrong role. Backpropagation computes the gradients; the optimiser uses those gradients to move θ.
fix: Backpropagation computes the gradient of the loss with respect to θ (1.9), and an optimiser such as gradient descent uses that gradient to update θ (Unit 2).

problem: 'Both paths end at the same test: score on rows held back from fitting' is accurate for the supervised path but loose for clustering. Held-out rows can be assigned to the nearest centre, yet there is no label to score against, so the check is a different one (cluster tightness, silhouette, business sense).
fix: Rewrite as: both paths are checked on rows not used in fitting — supervised by accuracy or error against held-back labels, unsupervised by how tight and separated the groups are on those rows.
